warmup.q: A payment's amount is 12x50, so reading it as a number fails every time. The ledger lets the error escape, which crashes it, and something restarts it at once. It saves its place in the log only after a whole batch of payments is done. What happens to the payments behind the bad one?
options: They're processed: Kafka skips a record that fails three times
They wait for as long as the code stays the same: every restart begins at the saved place, reaches the same payment and crashes again
Kafka moves the bad record aside after a few minutes
They move to another part of the log
warmup.why: Kafka doesn't know your code failed. A plain Kafka consumer has no limit on attempts and no dead-letter topic, a separate log for records it gave up on. Its saved place, the committed offset, stays before the bad record, so every restart reads again from there and fails at the same spot. A dead-letter topic exists only if your code, or a library you use, writes one. The first option is the tempting belief that Kafka gives up on a record for you. A queue program would at least count the attempts: RabbitMQ's quorum queues give up on a message after 20 deliveries by default and drop it, or move it to a dead-letter exchange if one is set. A Kafka consumer group counts nothing.

sections.h: One record that always fails stops its whole partition
sections.html:
Queues and brokers, the first lesson of this track, met the poison message: a message that crashes every consumer that takes it. The queue delivers it again, and it crashes the next one. On a log, the same record does more damage. Let's see why, and then build what the log leaves us to build ourselves.

First, the pieces. Each payment is a record in the Kafka topic payments, a named log, which Kafka splits into partitions: separate logs that each keep their own order. A consumer such as the ledger reads a partition in order, and saves a bookmark, the committed offset, to say how far it got.

Now pay-3 arrives with the amount 12x50. Somebody's payment form let a letter through. Turning that text into a number throws a NumberFormatException, and it will throw every time. (An exception is how Java and Kotlin report an error. This one means "that text isn't a number".)

Run it through the loop from Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees, which saves its bookmark only after a whole batch is done. The exception escapes before the commit, and the program crashes and is restarted. It starts at the committed offset, processes pay-0 to pay-2 again, reaches pay-3 and crashes again, forever. The Try-it below shows three rounds of it.

A kitchen has the same problem with its rail of order slips. The cook takes the slips in order. One slip is smudged and can't be read, and a cook who never skips a slip stands there while every order behind it waits.

A partition works like that rail. It has one bookmark per group, and the bookmark can only move past a record once the consumer is done with it. So one record that can't be done holds back everything behind it in its partition. If that partition receives 30 payments a second, 108,000 pile up behind pay-3 in an hour. The other partitions keep flowing, which makes it easy to miss: the group's total lag, how far behind it is, barely moves. A record that fails every time you process it is a poison pill.

Compare the queue from the first lesson. Its broker, the program that holds the messages, keeps a state for every message, so while a bad message is delivered again, the ones behind it go to other consumers. And the broker counts the attempts. Since RabbitMQ 4.0, a quorum queue (RabbitMQ's kind of queue that keeps copies on several machines) gives up after 20 deliveries by default. It drops the message, or moves it to a dead-letter exchange, a place for failed messages, if one is set. A Kafka consumer group keeps one bookmark per partition and counts nothing, so nothing gives up and nothing behind the record gets past. This is called head-of-line blocking: the first in line blocks the rest. It's the price of the log's order, and everything the queue's broker did for its poison message, a Kafka consumer has to do itself.

The failure can happen in two places. One is your own code, as here: a bad amount, a currency the ledger doesn't know, a missing value. The other is inside poll, in the deserializer, the code that turns a record's bytes back into an object your program can use. It fails when the bytes aren't what it expects, such as a damaged record, or a producer, the program that writes the records, that switched formats. Then poll hands out the good records in front of the bad one, and on the next call throws a RecordDeserializationException. The exception names the partition and the offset, and in Kafka 4.4 it also carries the record's raw key and value bytes. The consumer's position, its place in memory, stays on the bad record, so every later poll throws again. The only way past is seek(partition, offset + 1), which moves the position on by one. Seek without saving those bytes first, and the record is gone for good.

Before choosing a fix, ask why it failed, because the answer decides what helps.

A transient failure means the record is fine, and something around it was briefly wrong. The card's bank didn't answer in time, a database was busy, or another program answered "try again later" (an HTTP 503). The same call can work a second later, so retrying is right. In the kitchen, the oven isn't hot yet.

A permanent failure means the record, or your code, is wrong: 12x50, an unknown currency, a bug. Retrying fails the same way every time and only blocks the partition. That's the smudged slip.

The consumer has to tell the two apart, and its only clue is the exception's type. So make the list explicit: retry the exceptions you know are transient, and treat everything else as permanent. Next, we'll do both: retry a few times, then move the record out of the way.

try.title: Watch a poison pill stop a partition
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait. Docker is a tool that runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this starts one Kafka broker in one.

Run PoisonPillDemo (command below). It writes six amounts to a new topic, and the third is 12x50. Then it tries three times to get through them, each time with a fresh consumer that starts at the committed offset, as a restarted program would. Here, the code that handles each record turns the amount into a number.
Predict, then run it again with -Pargs=deserialize. Now the value deserializer turns the amount into a number, inside poll. On the third try, the demo seeks past the bad record.

Then a consumer that * restarts after every failure tries to get past it, three times. * Argument: "process" (the default: the handler parses the value and throws) or "deserialize" (the value * deserializer throws, inside poll; on the last try the consumer seeks past the bad record). */ public class PoisonPillDemo { /** Reads a payment amount in cents, "4000", from a record value. Throws on anything else. */ public static class AmountDeserializer implements Deserializer<Long> { @Override public Long deserialize(String topic, byte[] data) { return Long.parseLong(new String(data)); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean inDeserializer = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("deserialize"); String topic = "poison-" + System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000; // a new topic every run TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(topic, 0); try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092"))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(topic, 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); } try (var p = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class))) { for (String v : List.of("1000", "2500", "12x50", "4000", "990", "7000")) p.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, 0, "acct-7", v)).get(); } Map<String, Object> config = Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "group.id", "ledger-" + topic, "enable.auto.commit", false, "auto.offset.reset", "earliest"); for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) { // every attempt is a fresh consumer, as after a crash and a restart: it starts at the committed offset if (inDeserializer) { try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<>(config, new StringDeserializer(), new AmountDeserializer())) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); while (c.position(tp) < 6) { try { ConsumerRecords<String, Long> records = c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, Long> r : records) System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": offset " + r.offset() + " applied " + r.value() + " cents"); if (!records.isEmpty()) c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(c.position(tp)))); } catch (RecordDeserializationException e) { System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": poll threw " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " at offset " + e.offset() + " (" + e.getCause() + "); position stays " + c.position(tp)); if (attempt < 3) break; // crash: the next try starts at the committed offset c.seek(tp, e.offset() + 1); // the only way past it: skip the record c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(e.offset() + 1))); System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": seek to " + (e.offset() + 1) + ": offset " + e.offset() + " is skipped, and nobody will see it again"); } } } } else { try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<>(config, new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer())) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); try { while (c.position(tp) < 6) { ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { long cents = Long.parseLong(r.value()); // the handler: throws NumberFormatException on 12x50 System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": offset " + r.offset() + " applied " + cents + " cents"); } if (!records.isEmpty()) c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(c.position(tp)))); // after the whole batch } } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": crashed: " + e + "; no commit"); } } } } long committed; try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<>(config, new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer())) { OffsetAndMetadata om = c.committed(Set.of(tp)).get(tp); committed = om == null ? 0 : om.offset(); sections.h: Retry a few times, then move the record to a dead-letter topic
sections.html:
For a transient failure, the simplest fix is to try again on the spot, before moving on. Call the handler, the code that applies one payment, and if it throws a transient exception, wait and call it again. Two rules make this safe. Cap the attempts, at 3 for example, because a retry with no end is the poison pill again. And make the wait grow, 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms, so a struggling bank isn't hammered by every consumer at once. A wait that doubles each time is called exponential backoff. These retries run inside the poll loop, so all of them must fit inside max.poll.interval.ms, the 5 minutes a consumer may take between two polls (Consumer groups and rebalancing). Three tries with waits under a second are nothing. Six tries of 30 seconds each would use 3 of the 5 minutes.

When the attempts run out, or the failure is permanent, the consumer has to get the record out of the way. Printing an error message and committing past the record is tempting, and it loses the payment. One ledger entry goes missing, and nobody notices until someone checks the month's totals by hand. Instead, write the record to a dead-letter topic (DLT), such as payments.DLT. It gets the same key and value, plus headers that say where it came from and why it failed. In the kitchen, the smudged slip goes onto a problem tray with a note, and the cook moves on to the next slip.

A header is a small named value attached to a Kafka record, next to its key and value: a name in text and some bytes. Consumers that don't look at headers aren't affected by them. A useful dead letter carries the original topic, partition and offset, so someone can find the record and what was around it. It also carries the exception's class and message, so they know what to fix.

The order of the steps matters. Send the dead letter and wait for the broker to confirm it has it, which send(...).get() does. Only then commit the offset past the record:

Java
for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
    try {
        handleWithRetries(r);                        // transient failures: up to 3 attempts
    } catch (Exception e) {                          // permanent, or out of attempts
        dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, e, "payments.DLT")).get();   // acked before we move on
    }
}
consumer.commitSync(nextOffsets(records));           // only now is it safe to move the bookmark
Kotlin
for (r in records) {
    try {
        handleWithRetries(r)                         // transient failures: up to 3 attempts
    } catch (e: Exception) {                         // permanent, or out of attempts
        dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, e, "payments.DLT")).get()    // acked before we move on
    }
}
consumer.commitSync(nextOffsets(records))            // only now is it safe to move the bookmark

The two versions match line for line; Kotlin writes the type in catch after the name.

If the DLT write fails, nothing is committed. The batch comes back after a restart, and the dead letter is written then. That's the at-least-once rule from Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees, applied to failures. Move the bookmark only after the work is done, and here the work is the dead letter. Here, the log does better than the queue. A RabbitMQ quorum queue moves dead letters aside by itself, but by default at-most-once: if the place for dead letters can't take the message, it's gone. At-least-once dead-lettering there needs dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once together with overflow=reject-publish. In Kafka you write the dead letter yourself, so you choose the order, and confirming before you commit is at-least-once.

The name is a habit, not a rule. This lab uses payments.DLT. Spring for Apache Kafka 4, a popular library for Java programs that use Kafka, sends dead letters to payments-dlt by default, to the same partition number as the original. Whatever the name, a DLT needs an owner. It needs an alert when a record lands in it, and a replay tool that sends a fixed record back to payments. There, the ledger's idempotency key, a unique id per payment that lets it skip a repeat, keeps a replay from being applied twice.

A failure you log and skip is a payment you lose. Dead-letter it, and commit after.

Quick retries handle a hiccup. Next, we'll see what they can't handle: a bank that's down for minutes.

try.title: Retry, dead-letter, carry on
steps: Run DeadLetterDemo (command below). It writes eight payments to ledger-payments. The card's bank times out twice on pay-2, and pay-3, a payment from acct-7, has the amount 12x50. The consumer retries timeouts up to 3 times, sends whatever still fails to ledger-payments.DLT, and commits.
Predict which payments are applied, which are retried, and which end up in the DLT.

Read the DLT with its headers: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic ledger-payments.DLT --partition 0 --offset earliest --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.headers=true --timeout-ms 10000.

code.title: DeadLetterDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l09.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.OffsetAndMetadata; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.*; /** * Writes eight payments to partition 0 of "ledger-payments". The card issuer times out twice on pay-2, and pay-3, * acct-7's capture, is a poison pill: its amount is "12x50". The consumer retries a timeout up to 3 times, sends a * record that still fails to "ledger-payments.DLT" with headers that say where it came from, and moves on. * Argument: "skip" (the default: acct-7's later payments are processed) or "park" (they follow the failed one to * the DLT, so no payment of acct-7 overtakes it). */ public class DeadLetterDemo { /** The card issuer did not answer in time. Worth another try. */ static class IssuerTimeout extends RuntimeException { IssuerTimeout() { super("card issuer timed out"); } } static int issuerTimeouts = 2; static void handle(ConsumerRecord<String, String> r) { String[] f = r.value().split(","); if (f[0].equals("pay-2") && issuerTimeouts-- > 0) throw new IssuerTimeout(); Long.parseLong(f[2]); // throws NumberFormatException for 12x50: bad data, never worth a retry } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean park = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("park"); String topic = "ledger-payments"; String dlt = topic + ".DLT"; TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(topic, 0); try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092"))) { List<String> missing = new ArrayList<>(List.of(topic, dlt)); missing.removeAll(admin.listTopics().names().get()); if (!missing.isEmpty()) admin.createTopics(missing.stream().map(t -> new NewTopic(t, 1, (short) 1)).toList()).all().get(); } var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class)); String[][] payments = { {"acct-1", "pay-0,authorize,1000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-1,authorize,2500"}, {"acct-3", "pay-2,authorize,4000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-3,capture,12x50"}, {"acct-1", "pay-4,capture,1000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-5,refund,1250"}, {"acct-3", "pay-6,capture,4000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-7,authorize,3000"}}; long start = -1; for (String[] p : payments) { long offset = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, 0, p[0], p[1])).get().offset(); if (start < 0) start = offset; } Map<String, Long> parked = new HashMap<>(); // key -> offset of the failed record it waits behind try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "group.id", "ledger-dlt-demo", "enable.auto.commit", false, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); c.seek(tp, start); // this run's eight payments List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = new ArrayList<>(); while (records.size() < payments.length) records.addAll(c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).records(tp)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { String at = "offset " + r.offset() + " " + r.key() + " " + r.value() + ":"; Long behind = parked.get(r.key()); if (behind != null) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, "parked behind offset " + behind, "sfz.ParkedKey"); System.out.println(at + " parked behind offset " + behind + " -> " + dlt); continue; } for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) { try { handle(r); System.out.println(at + " applied" + (attempt > 1 ? " on attempt " + attempt : "")); break; } catch (IssuerTimeout e) { if (attempt == 3) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, e.getMessage(), e.getClass().getName()); System.out.println(at + " gave up after 3 attempts -> " + dlt); if (park) parked.put(r.key(), r.offset()); break; } long wait = 100L << (attempt - 1); // 100 ms, then 200 ms System.out.println(at + " attempt " + attempt + " failed (" + e.getMessage() + "), retry in " + wait + " ms"); Thread.sleep(wait); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, e.getMessage() == null ? "" : e.getMessage(), e.getClass().getName()); System.out.println(at + " " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", no retry -> " + dlt); if (park) parked.put(r.key(), r.offset()); break; } } } long next = records.get(records.size() - 1).offset() + 1; c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(next))); // after every dead letter is acked System.out.println("committed offset " + next + ": the partition is not stuck"); } producer.close(); } static void deadLetter(KafkaProducer<String, String> p, String dlt, ConsumerRecord<String, String> r, String why, String cls) throws Exception { var record = new ProducerRecord<>(dlt, r.key(), r.value()); record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", r.topic().getBytes()) .add("dlt.original.partition", Integer.toString(r.partition()).getBytes()) .add("dlt.original.offset", Long.toString(r.offset()).getBytes()) .add("dlt.exception.class", cls.getBytes()) .add("dlt.exception.message", why.getBytes()); p.send(record).get(); // wait for the broker's ack before the offset may be committed } }

sections.h: Long waits belong in retry topics, not in the poll loop
sections.html:
Retries on the spot handle a hiccup. They can't handle an outage, a stretch of time when a service is down. Say the card's bank is down for 3 minutes, while 30 payments arrive every second. Waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms give up in under a second. So every payment of those 3 minutes lands in the DLT: 5,400 records for a person to replay. Stretch the waits to 30 seconds and up to 6 attempts instead, and one payment holds its partition for 3 minutes. The payments behind it queue up, and the poll loop comes dangerously close to max.poll.interval.ms.

The fix is to wait somewhere else. A queue can make one message wait while the rest flow past. Since RabbitMQ 4.4, a message in a quorum queue can carry a time before which it won't be delivered. A log can't, because its bookmark is one number per partition. So Kafka consumers build the wait out of separate topics. Retry topics form a staircase of topics with growing delays: payments.retry-10s, then payments.retry-1m, then payments.DLT. When a record still fails after its quick retries, the main consumer writes it to payments.retry-10s, commits, and moves on to the next payment at full speed. Every record has a timestamp, the time it was written, so the retry consumer knows it's due 10 seconds after that.

A separate consumer group reads each retry topic. When the record at the head of a partition isn't due yet, the retry consumer doesn't sleep. It calls pause on that partition and keeps calling poll, which keeps it in its group (Consumer groups and rebalancing), while poll returns nothing for paused partitions. When the record is due, it calls resume, seeks back to the record and processes it. A failure there sends the record one step down the staircase, and the last step is the DLT. Every record in one retry topic waits the same 10 seconds, so they come due in the order they were written. The consumer only ever waits for the record at the head.

In the kitchen, it's a second rail for slips that wait for an ingredient to arrive. The cook pins the slip there with a time, carries on with the main rail, and comes back to it when the time comes.

Libraries build this staircase for you. Spring for Apache Kafka has @RetryableTopic, a label you put on a method to get the whole staircase. It's still worth knowing what these libraries do, because the staircase has a cost they can't hide. A record in a retry topic has left its partition, and the payments behind it carry on without it. For many kinds of record, that's fine. For a payment, it's a problem, and the next section deals with it.

sections.h: Keeping an account's payments in order: park the key
sections.html:
Look at acct-7 in the Try-it. A card payment can take up to three records. authorize asks the card's bank to set money aside, capture moves the money to the shop, and refund gives it back. pay-1 authorizes 25.00. pay-3 captures 12.50, but its amount is broken, so it goes to the DLT. pay-5 refunds the 12.50 and is applied: a refund of money that never moved. Next morning, someone fixes pay-3 and replays it, and the capture lands after its own refund.

Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering promised that one account's payments stay in order, because they share a key and so a partition. The DLT broke that promise for acct-7. A retry topic breaks it the same way, only for a shorter time. On the queue from Queues and brokers, the question hardly comes up, because competing consumers and redelivery mix up the order anyway. A log keeps the order of each key, so it's yours to lose.

The fix is to park the key. Once a record of acct-7 has gone to the DLT or a retry topic, every later record of acct-7 follows it there. Each carries a header naming the record it waits behind, until the first one is sorted out. Other accounts keep flowing. When pay-3 is fixed, the replay tool sends acct-7's three dead letters back in their original order. In the kitchen, once a table's main course slip goes to the problem tray, the same table's dessert slip goes there too, behind it.

In code, it's one check before the handler:

Java
String blockedBy = parked.get(r.key());
if (blockedBy != null) {
    dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, new ParkedKeyException(blockedBy), "payments.DLT")).get();
    continue;                                  // acct-7 waits behind its failed payment
}
Kotlin
val blockedBy = parked[r.key()]
if (blockedBy != null) {
    dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, ParkedKeyException(blockedBy), "payments.DLT")).get()
    continue                                   // acct-7 waits behind its failed payment
}

Both look the account up in parked, a map from an account to the record it waits behind. Kotlin reads the map with parked[r.key()] where Java calls get.

Where does the set of parked keys live? The lab keeps it in memory, and that isn't enough for a real ledger. After a restart, or after a rebalance moves the partition to another member (Consumer groups and rebalancing), the new consumer starts with an empty set. Then acct-7's next payment goes straight through. Keep the set where it survives, such as a table in the ledger's database. A compacted topic keyed by account works too: Kafka trims it to the newest record for each key (Partitions and segments on disk). Load it in onPartitionsAssigned, the function the consumer calls when it's given a partition.

Parking isn't always worth it. Some records don't depend on each other, such as receipt emails, or a record of who looked at what. For those, a little reordering does no harm, and you can let the rest through. Park whenever the records of a key build on each other: balances, steps that must come in order (authorize, capture, refund), and anything an idempotency check can't put back in order. And alert on parked accounts. Parking turns one bad record into one stuck customer, which is far better than a stuck partition, but it still needs a person.

When a key's records build on each other, one failure must hold the key. Park it.

Even with parking, every path in this lesson is at-least-once: a crash between applying a payment and committing still repeats it. That's where the next lesson picks up.

refs.title: KafkaConsumer (Kafka 4.4 javadoc): pause, resume and seek

opening:
Picture an ordinary Tuesday at the payments app. A shop's till sends a payment with the amount 12x50, a typing slip that a form let through. The ledger, the program that keeps each account's balance, tries to read it as a number and crashes. It restarts by itself, reads the same payment, and crashes again.

Every other account keeps flowing, so the screens look almost normal. But in that payment's part of the log, everything behind it waits: after an hour, 108,000 payments.

It's easy to think the system gives up on a bad message for you. Many queue programs do: they count the attempts and give up. Kafka, the program that keeps the log of payments for other programs to read, counts nothing.

In Consumer groups and rebalancing, we shared the work between consumers, one owner per partition. No owner can get past a record that always fails. In this lesson, we'll watch one stop its partition, sort failures into two kinds, move the bad record aside safely, and keep each account in order. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with one payment, 12x50, that crashed the ledger on every restart while 108,000 payments waited behind it. The fix had three parts. Retry what might clear by itself. Move what can't to a dead-letter topic, and commit only once it's safely there. And park the account, so its later payments wait in line behind the failed one.

Look at an app you use for something that failed, such as a photo that wouldn't upload. Does it retry by itself, set the photo aside with a reason, or quietly drop it?

Next, we'll follow a program that reads from Kafka and writes back to Kafka, and find out how Kafka can make its writes and its bookmark one step.

java.title: Java
java.html: static ProducerRecord<String, String> deadLetter(ConsumerRecord<String, String> failed, Throwable error, String dlt) { var record = new ProducerRecord<>(dlt, null, failed.key(), failed.value()); // partition from the key for (Header h : failed.headers()) record.headers().add(h); // keep the producer's headers record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", utf8(failed.topic())) .add("dlt.original.partition", utf8(Integer.toString(failed.partition()))) .add("dlt.original.offset", utf8(Long.toString(failed.offset()))) .add("dlt.exception.class", utf8(error.getClass().getName())) .add("dlt.exception.message", utf8(error.getMessage() == null ? "" : error.getMessage())); return record; } static byte[] utf8(String s) { return s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun deadLetter(failed: ConsumerRecord<String, String>, error: Throwable, dlt: String): ProducerRecord<String, String> { val record = ProducerRecord<String, String>(dlt, null, failed.key(), failed.value()) // partition from the key failed.headers().forEach { record.headers().add(it) } // keep the producer's headers record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", failed.topic().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.original.partition", failed.partition().toString().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.original.offset", failed.offset().toString().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.exception.class", error.javaClass.name.toByteArray()) .add("dlt.exception.message", (error.message ?: "").toByteArray()) return record }

compare.note: Header values are bytes in both languages, so every number becomes text first. Kotlin's toByteArray() uses UTF-8 by default. Java's getBytes() without an argument uses whatever character set the computer is set to, so the Java version passes UTF-8 itself. Kotlin's ?: replaces the check for a missing message: an Exception() made without a message gives null in both. In both, the partition is null, so the producer picks it from the key, and one account's dead letters stay together and in order.

steps.say: Write down which exceptions are transient. Everything not on the list is permanent, and goes to the DLT on the first failure. A list you can read on one screen beats a clever rule. If it happened first and the DLT write then failed, // the record would be in neither place: lost. With the ack first, a failed write means no commit, and the // record is read and dead-lettered again after a restart.

If it happened first and the DLT write then failed, // the record would be in neither place: lost. With the ack first, a failed write means no commit, and the // record is read and dead-lettered again after a restart.

recap: A record that fails every time (a poison pill) stops its partition: the bookmark can't pass it, and nothing counts the attempts. A queue's broker counts deliveries and gives up; a Kafka consumer must do that itself.
Sort failures by exception type. Retry transient ones a few times with exponential backoff, and send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once.
A dead letter keeps the key and value and adds headers: the original topic, partition and offset, and the exception. Wait for the broker to confirm it, then commit.
A record that can't be deserialized makes poll throw RecordDeserializationException on every call. Save its bytes, then seek past it.
Long waits go to retry topics with fixed delays, so the main partition keeps moving. For payments, park the key: an account's later records follow its failed one, in order.

The limit: every path here is still at-least-once. A crash between applying a payment and committing repeats it, so the ledger keeps its idempotency key, and a program that writes its results back to Kafka writes them twice.

explain.prompt: An alert fires: one partition of payments is 40,000 records behind and growing, while the other eleven are at 0. Explain what most likely happened, why the other partitions are fine, and what the consumer should do differently.
explain.answer: Most likely a poison pill: one record in that partition fails every time we process it, such as an amount we can't read as a number. Our consumer lets the exception escape before the commit, so it restarts at the committed offset, reaches the same record and fails again, forever. The bookmark can't move past it, so every payment written to that partition since then is waiting. The other partitions have their own bookmarks, so they keep flowing. The consumer should sort failures. It should retry the transient ones, like the bank timing out, a few times with backoff. It should send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once, with headers for the original topic, partition, offset and exception, wait for the broker to confirm that write, and then commit. Because these are payments, it should also park the account, so the account's later payments go to the DLT behind the failed one instead of overtaking it. The parked accounts belong in a table, so a restart doesn't forget them. Then someone fixes the record and replays the account's dead letters in order, and the idempotency keys make the replay safe.

deeper.html:
Saving records that can't be deserialized. When poll throws RecordDeserializationException, the exception holds everything you need to dead-letter the record without the deserializer: topicPartition(), offset(), timestamp(), headers(), and the raw keyBuffer() and valueBuffer(). Write those bytes to the DLT with a producer that sends raw bytes, then seek past. Another way is to read records as plain bytes and deserialize them in your handler, so a bad record becomes an ordinary handler failure. Spring's ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps a deserializer to do the same.

Retry topics without sleeping. The retry consumer's trick is pause(partitions) plus poll. A paused partition returns no records, but the loop keeps calling poll, so the member stays in its group and max.poll.interval.ms is never in danger. Store the due time in a header, or work it out from the record's timestamp, and resume the partition when the record at the head is due. Use one topic per delay. If a topic mixed 10-second and 10-minute delays, a 10-minute record at the head would hold back the 10-second records behind it.

Share groups and acknowledgements. Share groups and running Kafka in production covers share groups, where each record is acknowledged on its own. RELEASE returns a record for another attempt, REJECT gives up on it, and the broker counts deliveries (share.delivery.count.limit, 5 by default). Kafka 4.4 added a dead-letter queue on the broker for share groups (KIP-1191). Share groups give up the order of a key across consumers, so for payments the parking problem above stays yours.
